text: Chapter 1's lab modeled Harrow Logistics' order tracking application as four separate, disconnected CI records — the application, two servers, and a database — with nothing yet on the platform saying the application actually runs on its servers or depends on its database. This lab closes that gap, then uses the resulting graph for real impact analysis.

Three relationship records connect the four CIs. The application runs on WEB-HARROW-01 and runs on APP-HARROW-01, using the Runs on, Runs pair from Lesson 5. Its connection to Harrow Orders DB is different in kind — it depends on the database for data, not runs on it — so that record correctly uses Depends on, Used by instead, matching what's actually true.

With those three records in place, opening the Dependency View on the application shows two Runs on relationships and one Depends on relationship. Opening it on Harrow Orders DB instead shows the same data from the other side: one Used by relationship, pointing back at the application. Same records, two consistent views.

Now apply real impact analysis. Harrow Orders DB needs emergency maintenance for two hours. Starting at the database and walking outward: it's used by the Order Tracking Application, so taking it offline breaks the application itself, not just the database.

WEB-HARROW-01 and APP-HARROW-01 stay technically up — their relationships are Runs on, not a dependency on the database — but with the application they host broken, that uptime doesn't help anyone. The honest impact statement centers on the application, not the server hardware.

This chain legitimately stops at the application, because no CI yet represents the business service it supports — that's not a mistake, it's an accurate reflection of what's been built so far. Next, Chapter 3 introduces the Common Service Data Model specifically to add that missing layer, extending this exact chain one hop further.
